note.text: A soil profile is a vertical section showing horizons and underlying layers. O denotes predominantly organic litter where present. A is a mineral surface horizon often mixed with humified organic matter. B is an altered subsoil, sometimes showing accumulation from above. C is relatively little altered parent material; R is hard bedrock. An E horizon, where present, shows removal of substances such as clay or iron. Profiles vary: horizons may be absent, mixed or truncated, and C material need not match the rock immediately below.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to interpret labelled soil horizons and distinguish a profile model from every real soil sequence. Builds on: components, texture and structure. Leads to: topsoil loss and conservation decisions.

sections.heading: Follow the local example or model
sections.text: The drawing is an original idealised section, not a pit measured in Cameroon. Read from the surface down and distinguish mineral topsoil from organic litter. A cultivated or eroded profile near a settlement may lack an obvious O layer. Soil depth and horizon thickness require measured boundaries, not an estimate from the decorative thickness of this drawing.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Identify features as well as position. Do not diagnose a horizon from colour alone. Explain leaching as downward movement of soluble materials and eluviation as removal of substances from a horizon; accumulation can occur below. Observe supplied records on screen rather than entering roadside cuts or unstable pits.
